Simplify: Use the first retro template: break amide into aniline and heterocycle carboxylic acid. So we need to source:

- Heterocycle carboxylic acid: c2nnn(Cc3ccc(CN4CC(F)C4)cc3)c2N attached to carbonyl. So the heterocycle is a 1,2,4-triazine with an amino substituent and a side chain (aryl-CH2-N-azetidine). The carboxylic acid is attached to the heterocycle at the carbonyl carbon. So the heterocycle carboxylic acid SMILES: O=C(c2nnn(Cc3ccc(CN4CC(F)C4)cc3)c2N)?? Actually the carboxylic acid would be O=C(O)c2nnn(Cc3ccc(CN4CC(F)C4)cc3)c2N. So we need that as a precursor.

We can further retro this heterocycle carboxylic acid using another template maybe breaking the C-C bond to the side chain? Or we could source the heterocycle carboxylic acid directly as a commercial chemical? Might be not common.

We can consider a different disconnection: break the C-C bond between the heterocycle and the phenyl side chain (the Cc3ccc...). That could give the heterocycle with a hydrogen (or something) and a benzyl halide that can be attached later.

Actually the forward would be coupling of heterocycle NH with benzyl bromide to give CH2 attached to heterocycle. So we can use that: break the C-CH2 bond between heterocycle and phenyl ring, giving benzyl bromide (or bromomethyl aryl) and heterocycle NH (the heterocycle with NH). That seems plausible.

Thus we can have a 3-step route:

Step 1 (retro): Break amide -> aniline (p-anisidine) + heterocycle carboxylic acid (with NH and side chain still attached). But we might further break heterocycle carboxylic acid into heterocycle core (triazine) and side chain.

Alternatively, we could break the heterocycle carboxylic acid into heterocycle core (triazine) and a carboxylic acid? Actually the heterocycle carboxylic acid is the core with side chain attached. Could we source the heterocycle core (triazine) with amino and side chain? Might be complex.

Maybe better to use a different disconnection: break the amide and also break the C-CH2 bond to give simpler fragments: aniline (p-anisidine) and benzyl bromide (or benzyl halide) and heterocycle with NH and carboxylic acid? Wait the heterocycle carboxylic acid still contains the side chain attached via CH2 to phenyl. If we break that CH2 bond, we get heterocycle with NH and carboxylic acid (no side chain) and a benzyl bromide (aryl-CH2-Br). Then we can later attach the side chain via SN2.

Thus overall route:

Target -> (retro amide) gives aniline (p-anisidine) + heterocycle carboxylic acid (with side chain). Then heterocycle carboxylic acid -> (retro C-CH2 bond) gives heterocycle carboxylic acid without side chain (i.e., O=C(O)c2nnn(N)c2N? Actually the heterocycle with NH and carboxylic acid) + benzyl bromide (bromomethyl phenyl with N4CC(F)C4 substituent). Then we can assemble: first couple heterocycle carboxylic acid with aniline to form amide (step 1). Then perform SN2 of heterocycle NH (maybe after deprotonation) with benzyl bromide to attach side chain (step 2). That's total 2 steps forward synthesis. Leaves: p-anisidine, heterocycle carboxylic acid (no side chain), benzyl bromide with side chain (aryl-CH2-Br). Are those commercially available? p-anisidine yes. Benzyl bromide with side chain maybe not common. The side chain is Cc3ccc(CN4CC(F)C4)cc3 (a phenyl with a side chain containing N-azetidine). That whole aryl-CH2-Br might not be commercially available.

Alternative: Use a different disconnection: attach the side chain via reductive amination of a benzaldehyde with the azetidine amine. So we could have benzaldehyde (para-methoxy phenyl with CH2-? Actually the side chain is attached to phenyl via CH2 (benzyl). So we could have 4-methoxybenzaldehyde (p-anisaldehyde) and then do reductive amination with the amine (CN4CC(F)C4). But the side chain is attached to the phenyl ring via CH2 attached to N4CC(F)C4 (i.e., a benzyl amine). So we could have 4-methoxybenzyl bromide and then substitute with azetidine amine. That might be more feasible: benzyl bromide (p-anisyl bromide) is commercially available. Then SN2 with azetidine amine (maybe N-Boc-azetidine? but we need N4CC(F)C4). That specific fluorinated azetidine may be commercially available.

2. 4-methoxybenzyl bromide (COc1ccc(CBr)cc1) (or 4-methoxybenzyl chloride)
